title: CSS Selectors and XPath in Playwright
excerpt: Playwright's built-in locators should be your first choice when finding elements. But in real projects, you'll sometimes need CSS selectors or XPath. In this part, we'll learn when to use each approach and practice them using the SauceDemo login page.
html:
CSS Selectors and XPath

In the previous part, we learned how to find elements using Playwright's recommended locators such as:

getByRole()
getByPlaceholder()
getByTestId()

These should normally be your first choice.

But when working with real applications, you'll sometimes inspect an element and find that a CSS selector or XPath is useful.

Let's see how they work and, more importantly, when you should use them.

Create a New Test File

Inside the tests folder, create:

tests/selectors.spec.ts

Add this basic setup:

import { test } from "@playwright/test";

test("Practice CSS selectors and XPath", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com/");
});

We'll use this file for the examples in this article.

When Should I Use Playwright Locators?

Start with Playwright's built-in locators whenever possible.

For example, SauceDemo has a Username field with the placeholder Username.

We can find it using:

const usernameInput = page.getByPlaceholder("Username");

For the Login button:

const loginButton = page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

These are good choices because they describe the element in a way that's easy to understand.

You should normally try these first:

getByRole()
getByLabel()
getByPlaceholder()
getByText()
getByAltText()
getByTitle()
getByTestId()

The idea is simple:

Use a locator that clearly describes the element and is likely to remain stable.

When Should I Use CSS Selectors?

Use a CSS selector when a Playwright built-in locator doesn't give you a good option, or when the element has a useful and stable HTML attribute.

For example, the SauceDemo Username field has:

<input id="user-name">

We can use the CSS ID selector:

const usernameInput = page.locator("#user-name");

Here:

#user-name

is the CSS selector. The # means we're selecting an element by its ID.

We can then interact with it:

await page.locator("#user-name").fill("standard_user");

CSS selectors can also use classes.

If an element has:

class="submit-button"

we can use:

page.locator(".submit-button");

The . means we're selecting an element by its class.

Be careful with classes, though. Classes are often used for styling, and developers may change them when the UI design changes.

A stable ID or test-specific attribute is generally a better choice.

CSS Attribute Selectors

CSS can also find elements using their attributes.

SauceDemo has:

<input data-test="username">

We can use:

const usernameInput = page.locator('[data-test="username"]');

This is a CSS attribute selector.

Since data-test is being used to identify the element for testing, it can be a good choice.

However, Playwright already provides:

page.getByTestId("username");

So if your Playwright project is configured to use data-test as its test ID attribute, getByTestId() is usually easier to read.

The important lesson is:

Don't use locator() just because you can.

If a Playwright locator gives you the same result in a clearer way, prefer it.

A Real CSS Example with SauceDemo

Let's create a complete login test using CSS selectors.

Replace the test in selectors.spec.ts with:

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("Login using CSS selectors", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com/");

  await page.locator("#user-name").fill("standard_user");
  await page.locator("#password").fill("secret_sauce");
  await page.locator("#login-button").click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/inventory/);
});

This test:

  1. Opens SauceDemo.

  2. Finds the Username field using its ID.

  3. Finds the Password field using its ID.

  4. Finds the Login button using its ID.

  5. Logs in.

  6. Checks that the URL contains inventory.

The test works, but remember:

Just because a locator works doesn't mean it's automatically the best locator.

For example, this:

page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

is usually easier to understand than:

page.locator("#login-button");

Both can work, but the first one describes the element from the user's point of view.

What About XPath?

XPath is another way to find elements in HTML.

For example, SauceDemo's Login button contains:

<input id="login-button" value="Login">

We could find it using:

const loginButton = page.locator("//input[@id='login-button']");

The XPath:

//input[@id='login-button']

basically means:

Find an input element whose id is login-button.

We can then click it:

await page.locator("//input[@id='login-button']").click();

That's enough XPath knowledge for now.

You don't need to memorize complicated XPath syntax at this stage. The important thing is understanding what XPath is and when it can be useful.

How to Write a Custom XPath

You don't need to memorize complicated XPath expressions. The easiest way to learn XPath is to build it step by step from the HTML.

Let's use the SauceDemo Login button:

<input
  type="submit"
  class="submit-button btn_action"
  data-test="login-button"
  id="login-button"
  value="Login">

Start with the element

The element is:

<input>

So our XPath starts with:

//input

The // means:

Find this type of element anywhere in the page.

So:

//input

means:

Find an input element anywhere on the page.

Find it using an attribute

The input has:

id="login-button"

We can add that attribute:

//input[@id='login-button']

Read it like this:

Find an input whose id is login-button.

That's our custom XPath.

We can use it in Playwright:

const loginButton = page.locator("//input[@id='login-button']");

Using another attribute

We could also use the data-test attribute:

data-test="login-button"

So the XPath becomes:

//input[@data-test='login-button']

And in Playwright:

const loginButton = page.locator(
  "//input[@data-test='login-button']"
);

Both XPath expressions can find the same element.

Using Text

XPath can also find elements based on their text.

For example, imagine we have:

<button>Login</button>

We could write:

//button[text()='Login']

This means:

Find a button whose text is Login.

In Playwright:

const loginButton = page.locator("//button[text()='Login']");

This can be useful when the visible text uniquely identifies the element.

Using contains()

Sometimes the exact value isn't known or the text contains additional content.

For example:

<button>Login to your account</button>

Instead of matching the entire text, we can use:

//button[contains(text(),'Login')]

This means:

Find a button whose text contains Login.

contains() is useful when you only know part of the value.

Using Multiple Attributes

Sometimes one attribute isn't enough to uniquely identify an element.

For example:

<input
  type="text"
  name="username"
  placeholder="Username">

We can combine attributes:

//input[@type='text' and @name='username']

Read it as:

Find an input that is type text AND has the name username.

In Playwright:

const usernameInput = page.locator(
  "//input[@type='text' and @name='username']"
);

A Simple XPath Pattern to Remember

Most of the XPath you'll need at this stage follows a simple pattern:

//element[@attribute='value']

For example:

//input[@id='user-name']

or:

//button[@type='submit']

If you need two conditions:

//input[@type='text' and @name='username']

If you're looking for specific text:

//button[text()='Login']

If you only know part of the text:

//button[contains(text(),'Login')]

That's enough to get started with custom XPath.

You don't need to memorize every XPath function right now. Start with these patterns and practice creating them from the HTML you see in Developer Tools.

Practice: Write the XPath Yourself

Open SauceDemo and inspect the Username input.

You should see something similar to:

<input
  placeholder="Username"
  type="text"
  data-test="username"
  id="user-name"
  name="user-name">

Now try to create an XPath that finds the Username field using its name attribute.

Think about it step by step:

1. What is the element?
2. Which attribute should I use?
3. What is the attribute value?

Your XPath should follow this pattern:

//element[@attribute='value']

Practice Solution

The element is:

input

The attribute is:

name

The value is:

user-name

So the XPath is:

//input[@name='user-name']

And in Playwright:

const usernameInput = page.locator("//input[@name='user-name']");

The more you inspect HTML and write these simple expressions yourself, the easier XPath will become.

CSS or XPath?

If you need to use locator(), a simple CSS selector is often easier to read than a complicated XPath.

For example:

page.locator("#login-button");

is much easier to understand than:

page.locator("//form/div[3]/input");

Both might find the same element, but the first one is easier to maintain.

Avoid Long and Fragile Selectors

This is something you'll come across when inspecting real websites.

Your browser's Developer Tools might show you a selector such as:

#app > div > div:nth-child(2) > div > form > div > button

It might work today, but it depends heavily on the current HTML structure.

If a developer adds another div or changes the layout, your test can break.

The same problem happens with long XPath expressions.

For example:

/html/body/div/div/div/form/div[3]/input

Try to avoid selectors like these.

Instead, inspect the element and look for something meaningful and stable:

  • Role

  • Label

  • Placeholder

  • Test ID

  • Stable ID

  • Stable custom attribute

Don't simply copy the longest selector that Developer Tools gives you.

How Do I Pick a Stable Locator?

Let's look at the actual SauceDemo Login button.

Its HTML contains:

<input
  type="submit"
  class="submit-button btn_action"
  data-test="login-button"
  id="login-button"
  value="Login">

There are several ways we could locate it.

Using a Playwright locator:

page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

Using a test ID:

page.getByTestId("login-button");

Using a CSS ID:

page.locator("#login-button");

Using XPath:

page.locator("//input[@id='login-button']");

All of these can locate the same element.

But they aren't equally good choices.

For this particular button, I would start with:

page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

because it clearly describes what the user sees and interacts with.

The test ID is also a good option if your project uses test IDs as a stable automation strategy.

A Simple Locator Decision Rule

When you need to find an element, use this order:

1. Try a Playwright locator

Ask yourself:

Can I identify this element using its role, label, placeholder, text, or test ID?

If yes, use it.

For example:

page.getByRole("button", { name: "Login" });

2. If not, look for a stable CSS selector

For example:

page.locator("#user-name");

or:

page.locator('[data-test="username"]');

3. If CSS isn't practical, consider XPath

For example:

page.locator("//input[@id='login-button']");

So remember:

Playwright locator first → CSS when useful → XPath when necessary.

You don't need to use CSS or XPath just to prove that you know them.

The goal is to find the element in a clear and stable way.

Practice

Now create a new file inside the tests folder:

tests/selector-practice.spec.ts

Use the SauceDemo login page.

Write a test that:

  1. Opens SauceDemo.

  2. Finds the Username field using a CSS ID selector.

  3. Finds the Password field using a CSS attribute selector.

  4. Finds the Login button using XPath.

  5. Enters the username and password.

  6. Clicks Login.

  7. Checks that the URL contains inventory.

Try writing the test yourself before looking at the solution.

Practice Solution

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("Practice CSS and XPath selectors", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com/");

  await page.locator("#user-name").fill("standard_user");
  await page.locator('[data-test="password"]').fill("secret_sauce");
  await page.locator("//input[@id='login-button']").click();

  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/inventory/);
});

Here we deliberately used three different approaches.

Username:

page.locator("#user-name");

CSS ID selector.

Password:

page.locator('[data-test="password"]');

CSS attribute selector.

Login button:

page.locator("//input[@id='login-button']");

XPath. The purpose of this exercise is not to make you use CSS and XPath everywhere.

It's to make sure you understand how they work when you encounter them in a real project.

One Rule to Remember

When you inspect an element, don't immediately ask:

"What CSS selector or XPath can I write?"

First ask:

"What is the clearest and most stable way to identify this element?"

If a Playwright locator gives you a good answer, use it. If not, look for a stable CSS selector. If CSS isn't practical, XPath can be useful.

A good locator isn't the longest or most complicated one.

It's the one that clearly identifies the element and is less likely to break when the application changes.
